docs.text: Chapter 3: Biblical anthropology, nature and person, the image of God, union with Christ, and the nous Thesis Biblical anthropology, illumined by the Christological distinction between person ( hypostasis ) and nature ( physis ), discloses humanity as created in the image of God, wounded by sin, and renewed through union with Christ by the Spirit. This chapter argues that (1) the gospel includes both the objective healing and glorification of human nature in the incarnate Son and (2) the personal transformation of each human hypostasis by the Holy Spirit, especially through the renewal of the nous within the ecclesial Ordo of Word–Table–Prayer. The Spirit’s renewal is enacted as a training of attention that re‑forms desire, so that the image may advance toward its eschatological telos of divine likeness. Biblical Ground (Primary Texts) Genesis 1:26–27 John 1:14 Luke 24:45 Romans 12:2 2 Corinthians 3:18 Colossians 3:10 In Genesis 1:26–27, humanity is created “in our image, according to our likeness,” establishing a relational and vocational anthropology in which human beings are addressed by God and entrusted with participation in his rule. John 1:14 reveals the incarnate Son as the one who assumes human nature itself, so that our being may be healed and glorified in him. Luke 24:45 and Romans 12:2 link salvation to the renewal of the nous —the “mind” or spiritual perception—while 2 Corinthians 3:18 and Colossians 3:10 depict believers as being transformed into Christ’s image and clothed with a renewed humanity. Together these texts ground an account of the image as wounded yet real, and of salvation as participatory renewal in Christ through the Spirit. Chapter Body I. Context and Question at Issue Modern accounts of “the self” are often fragmented and reductive. In many cultural and pastoral settings, the human person is implicitly treated either as a psychological interior (a bundle of experiences and feelings), as a biological organism (a sophisticated animal whose behavior can be fully explained by brain and body), or as a voluntarist agent (a will that defines itself by its choices). Each of these partial views captures something important, but none can function as an adequate Christian anthropology. By contrast, Scripture begins not with self-analysis but with a divine address: “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness” (Gen 1:26). Humanity is immediately presented as relational and vocational—called into communion with God, given a task within creation, and defined not by interior states or sheer choice but by a received identity before God. The fall does not erase this identity, but disorders it. Human nature remains human; the image remains real; yet desire is misdirected, perception is darkened, and the path from image to likeness is obstructed. Pastorally, this means that if the Church simply adopts the surrounding culture’s anthropology, the gospel is inevitably reduced. Without a biblically and christologically grounded vision of the human person, proclamation collapses either into moralism (“try harder, do better”) or into therapy (“feel better, cope more successfully”). Discipleship becomes a technique rather than a participation in Christ. The more urgent question, then, is not “How do I feel about myself?” but “Who am I before God, and what am I for in light of Christ and the Spirit’s work?” Section Summary: This chapter arises from the collision between fragmented modern images of the self and Scripture’s claim that humanity is addressed by God, bears his image, and is called into renewed communion in Christ. The central question is: What is the human person in light of Christ—one person in two natures—and the Spirit’s work of conforming us to him? Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: the “self” is a psychological interior, a biological mechanism, or a choosing will. After: the person is a hypostasis of human nature addressed by God, created in the image, and ordered to communion and likeness in Christ. II. Prior Answers and Their Inadequacy Long before explicit secular anthropologies, Christian practice itself has sometimes fallen into reductionist patterns. One common tendency is to equate the person with interior experience: “I am what I feel.” Here the goal of ministry becomes managing or optimizing emotions, and the gospel becomes a promise of inward equilibrium. Another tendency is to reduce the person to moral performance: “I am what I do.” Holiness is measured by visible compliance, and salvation is functionally framed as behavior management. A third reduction leans toward materialism: “I am my body and brain.” Human beings are treated as complex biological systems, and spiritual language becomes either metaphorical or marginal. Each of these impulses contains a partial truth: feelings matter; actions matter; embodiment matters. Yet taken as governing frames, they cannot sustain a properly Christian account of salvation. If the self is exhausted by feeling or performance, then salvation will be imagined merely as emotional relief or moral improvement. If the human being is only a biological machine, then talk of communion with God, deification, or participation in Christ becomes unintelligible. In each case, ecclesial life shrinks: worship is reduced to inspiration, ethics to technique, and pastoral care to adjustment. These prior answers also neglect the ecclesial, sacramental, and eschatological dimensions of the gospel. The Church becomes a support group or an ethical society, rather than the body that participates in Christ’s healed humanity and lives toward the resurrection. The sacraments are treated as symbols of our inner states rather than as means by which the Spirit unites us to Christ. The eschatological horizon of likeness to God is obscured behind immediate needs and projects. Section Summary: Psychological, moralistic, and materialist reductions each grasp something real but finally prove inadequate: they cannot sustain Scripture’s portrayal of humanity as image-bearing, sin-wounded, and ordered to participation in God through Christ and the Spirit. These frames truncate both the scope of salvation and the depth of ecclesial life. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: “salvation” is emotional relief, moral performance, or successful coping within the limits of the present age. After: salvation is participation in Christ’s healed humanity, within the Church, ordered toward deification and resurrection. III. The Scriptural Event or Claim Genesis 1:26–27 announces the human as created in the image and likeness of God. From the beginning, humanity is constituted by divine address, entrusted with dominion, and oriented toward a destiny of likeness. This is not a static possession but a vocation: to grow into the likeness of the God whose image we bear. Even after the fall, Scripture never says that the image is lost; rather, the image is wounded and obscured. Human life now unfolds under conditions of misdirected desire, distorted perception, and disordered rule. The gospel does not begin with human striving but with God’s decisive act: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). In Jesus Christ, the eternal Son assumes our nature without ceasing to be who he is. His life, death, and resurrection manifest human nature as it is meant to be—filial, eucharistic, and oriented wholly to the Father. In him we see not an escape from created finitude, but a redeemed and glorified humanity that is the template and source of our renewal. Scripture ties this renewal to a transformation of perception and understanding. The risen Christ “opened their minds ( nous ) to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45), and Paul exhorts believers: “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind ( nous )” (Rom 12:2). Here the nous is not bare intellect but the deep “eye of the heart” by which the whole person attends to reality. As we behold “the glory of the Lord” we are “being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Cor 3:18); we “have stripped off the old self with its practices and have clothed [ourselves] with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator” (Col 3:9–10). Section Summary: Scripture presents humanity as created in God’s image and called to likeness, wounded but not erased by sin, and renewed through the incarnate Son who assumes and perfects our nature and opens the nous to God’s reality. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: the human problem is primarily behavioral or emotional, requiring better rules or better feelings. After: the human problem is a wounded image and darkened nous ; the solution is God’s assumption and renewal of our nature in Christ, and the Spirit’s transformation of perception and desire. IV. Patristic Reading and Insight The patristic tradition reads Genesis and the gospel narratives not as isolated texts but as parts of a single economy of salvation. A widespread interpretation distinguishes between “image” and “likeness”: the image is a structural gift given in creation, while likeness is an eschatological telos —the journey into mature communion with God. Gregory of Nyssa , in On the Making of Man , portrays human life as an infinite progression into divine likeness, grounded in the unlosable image. Within this broad consensus, one influential strand—especially in Maximus the Confessor —discerns within the image a triadic pattern corresponding to a kind of Trinitarian anthropology: nous , logos , and pneuma . The nous is the spiritual perception or “eye of the heart”; the logos is rational articulation and meaning-making; and the pneuma is the vital dynamism of the person in love and movement. Sin is thus more than rule-breaking: it is the misorientation of the whole human life—clouded nous , distorted logos , dissipated pneuma . Athanasius famously summarizes the incarnational horizon: “God became man that man might become god” ( On the Incarnation 54). Deification ( theosis ) does not mean absorption into the divine essence, but participation in God’s life through the Son’s restored humanity. Augustine , Cyril of Alexandria , and John of Damascus each, in distinctive ways, emphasize that the image’s healing and elevation occur in and through Christ, within the Church, by the Spirit. Taken together, the Fathers read Scripture as revealing an anthropology ordered to deification, grounded in Christ’s person and work. Section Summary: The Fathers discern in Scripture an anthropology in which the image is retained but wounded, ordered to likeness, and structured by nous–logos–pneuma ; they interpret Christ’s incarnate and deifying work as the healing and elevation of this image within the Church. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: modern habits read Scripture as a set of religious ideas about an isolated individual self. After: the Church’s patristic reading unveils a coherent economy in which human nous–logos–pneuma are healed and deified through union with the incarnate Son. V. Doctrinal Synthesis (Resolution) The Council of Chalcedon (451) confesses Christ as one divine person ( hypostasis ) in two natures ( physeis ), “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.” This distinction clarifies that nature answers the question what something is, while person answers who . Applied to anthropology, it yields two guardrails: we must neither reduce persons to functions (psychology, biology, or sheer will) nor treat “person” as a disembodied ghost. A human person is an irreducible “who” who subsists as embodied, ensouled human nature. Christ is the key. In him, the eternal “who” of the Son truly assumes the human “what” of our nature without diminishing either. The gospel, then, is not the rescue of souls from bodies, nor the enhancement of a generic spirituality, but the healing and glorification of humanity in the incarnate Son. Here we can distinguish an objective and a personal dimension: objectively, human nature is healed, clarified, and perfected in the economy of the incarnate Word; personally, each human hypostasis is united to Christ and transformed by the Spirit. Deification thus has both a Christological center and a pneumatological extension. This doctrinal synthesis allows a non-reductionist anthropology. The person is more than psyche, body, or will, yet never exists apart from them. Human nature, assumed and renewed in Christ, is the site where salvation is enacted; persons participate in this renewed nature through union with Christ by the Spirit, especially in the Church’s sacramental and liturgical life. Chalcedonian Christology thus becomes a key for understanding both who the human person is and how salvation truly heals and elevates our being. Section Summary: By reading Scripture with the Church, we arrive at a Chalcedonian anthropology: persons are irreducible “who’s” who subsist in human nature; this nature is assumed, healed, and glorified in Christ; and each person is called to participate personally in this renewed humanity through the Spirit. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: we could not speak coherently about salvation without either collapsing the person into nature (biology, psychology, will) or dissolving nature into a vague “self.” After: we can confess and live an anthropology in which human nature is objectively renewed in Christ and each person is personally united to him by the Spirit. VI. Anthropological and Spiritual Implications If salvation includes both the healing of human nature in Christ and the transformation of persons by the Spirit, then Christian formation cannot be reduced to moral effort or doctrinal information. Scripture’s language of nous points to a deeper transformation: “Then he opened their minds ( nous ) to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45); “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind ( nous )” (Rom 12:2). The nous is the faculty of spiritual perception by which the whole person attends to and receives reality in God. Its renewal therefore reorders every dimension of life. Attention is the hinge between illumination and desire. What the nous repeatedly attends to becomes what the heart comes to want. Attention is never neutral: scattered attention leaves desire at the mercy of fear, novelty, and passion; gathered attention trains desire toward freedom in Christ. As the Spirit illumines the nous , the logos is re-directed toward truthful confession and wise action, and the pneuma is vivified toward love, endurance, and worship. In this way, nature is renewed in Christ, and persons are progressively conformed to him. Spiritual disciplines, then, are best understood as practices of Spirit-enabled attentiveness rather than self-improvement techniques. Catechesis becomes an initiation into a new way of seeing—learning to perceive oneself and the world in Christ. Pastoral care addresses not only behavior or feeling but the deeper question of who the person is before God and how their nous–logos–pneuma are being drawn into Christ’s pattern of life. Section Summary: The renewal of the nous by the Spirit reorders attention, desire, and practice so that human persons may participate in Christ’s healed humanity; formation is an apprenticeship in attentiveness rather than a project of self-optimization. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: “change” is primarily a matter of willpower, technique, or therapeutic adjustment. After: change is Spirit-enabled participation in Christ, enacted through the renewal of the nous and the re-forming of desire. VII. Ecclesial and Liturgical Location The Church’s worship is not ornament but ontology: in Word, Table, and Prayer the Spirit enacts and sustains our participation in Christ’s humanity. The liturgy is the Spirit’s school of personhood, where attention is gathered, desire is re-formed, and the image is led toward likeness. In the Eucharist, anamnesis is more than recollection; it is participation in the saving economy made present. In epiclesis , the Church calls upon the Spirit not simply to bless bread and wine, but to make us sharers in Christ—to receive not abstractions or “benefits” only, but communion with the crucified and risen Lord. Baptismal epiclesis similarly marks personal incorporation into Christ, where the Spirit seals each hypostasis into the renewed humanity of the Son. The Ordo—Word, Table, Prayer forms a pedagogy of desire by training attention. The Word gathers the nous , teaching it where to look and how to see reality in God’s light. The Table concentrates attention upon Christ’s self-giving presence, redirecting desire from possession to participation. Prayer sustains and purifies attention over time, integrating the whole person into doxology, repentance, and intercession. Here discipleship becomes participatory rather than performative: the Church learns not only what to do but what to be—humanity in Christ. Frame Reinforcement Loop (1–2 sentences): The Church does not merely express doctrine in worship; she re-installs the gospel’s frame of reality week by week. In Word, Table, and Prayer, the Spirit stabilizes a Christocentric anthropology in which persons learn to see, desire, and act from within Christ’s healed humanity. Section Summary: Through baptismal incorporation, Eucharistic participation, and the Ordo of Word–Table–Prayer, the Church becomes the concrete place where the doctrine of renewed humanity is embodied, transmitted, and reinforced as the Spirit’s pedagogy of attention and desire. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: worship is a periodic expression of religious feeling or inspiration. After: worship is the Spirit’s pedagogy that stabilizes the gospel’s frame of reality in persons and communities, training nous–logos–pneuma for participation in Christ. Spiritual Formation: Emphasize the renewal of the nous through Scripture, sacrament, and prayer, distinguishing this deep spiritual perception from mere information transfer or technique. Pastoral Care: Address reductionist views of the self—moralistic, therapeutic, or materialist—by offering a vision of healed nature and transformed personhood in which each hypostasis is called to participate in Christ’s deified humanity. Objections & Replies Objection: Does focusing on the nous privilege intellect over the body and everyday life? Reply: No. The nous is not bare intellect but the “eye of the heart,” the integrative faculty by which the embodied person is oriented toward God. Chapter 3: Biblical anthropology, nature and person, the image of God, union with Christ, and the nous

docs.text: Biblical anthropology, illumined by the Christological distinction between person ( hypostasis ) and nature ( physis ), discloses humanity as created in the image of God, wounded by sin, and renewed through union with Christ by the Spirit. This chapter argues that (1) the gospel includes both the objective healing and glorification of human nature in the incarnate Son and (2) the personal transformation of each human hypostasis by the Holy Spirit, especially through the renewal of the nous within the ecclesial Ordo of Word–Table–Prayer. The Spirit’s renewal is enacted as a training of attention that re‑forms desire, so that the image may advance toward its eschatological telos of divine likeness.
docs.title: Thesis

docs.text: Genesis 1:26–27 John 1:14 Luke 24:45 Romans 12:2 2 Corinthians 3:18 Colossians 3:10 In Genesis 1:26–27, humanity is created “in our image, according to our likeness,” establishing a relational and vocational anthropology in which human beings are addressed by God and entrusted with participation in his rule. John 1:14 reveals the incarnate Son as the one who assumes human nature itself, so that our being may be healed and glorified in him. Luke 24:45 and Romans 12:2 link salvation to the renewal of the nous —the “mind” or spiritual perception—while 2 Corinthians 3:18 and Colossians 3:10 depict believers as being transformed into Christ’s image and clothed with a renewed humanity. Together these texts ground an account of the image as wounded yet real, and of salvation as participatory renewal in Christ through the Spirit.
docs.title: Biblical Ground (Primary Texts)
Chapter Body

docs.text: Modern accounts of “the self” are often fragmented and reductive. In many cultural and pastoral settings, the human person is implicitly treated either as a psychological interior (a bundle of experiences and feelings), as a biological organism (a sophisticated animal whose behavior can be fully explained by brain and body), or as a voluntarist agent (a will that defines itself by its choices). Each of these partial views captures something important, but none can function as an adequate Christian anthropology. By contrast, Scripture begins not with self-analysis but with a divine address: “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness” (Gen 1:26). Humanity is immediately presented as relational and vocational—called into communion with God, given a task within creation, and defined not by interior states or sheer choice but by a received identity before God. The fall does not erase this identity, but disorders it. Human nature remains human; the image remains real; yet desire is misdirected, perception is darkened, and the path from image to likeness is obstructed. Pastorally, this means that if the Church simply adopts the surrounding culture’s anthropology, the gospel is inevitably reduced. Without a biblically and christologically grounded vision of the human person, proclamation collapses either into moralism (“try harder, do better”) or into therapy (“feel better, cope more successfully”). Discipleship becomes a technique rather than a participation in Christ. The more urgent question, then, is not “How do I feel about myself?” but “Who am I before God, and what am I for in light of Christ and the Spirit’s work?” Section Summary: This chapter arises from the collision between fragmented modern images of the self and Scripture’s claim that humanity is addressed by God, bears his image, and is called into renewed communion in Christ. The central question is: What is the human person in light of Christ—one person in two natures—and the Spirit’s work of conforming us to him? Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: the “self” is a psychological interior, a biological mechanism, or a choosing will. After: the person is a hypostasis of human nature addressed by God, created in the image, and ordered to communion and likeness in Christ.
docs.title: I. Context and Question at Issue

docs.text: Long before explicit secular anthropologies, Christian practice itself has sometimes fallen into reductionist patterns. One common tendency is to equate the person with interior experience: “I am what I feel.” Here the goal of ministry becomes managing or optimizing emotions, and the gospel becomes a promise of inward equilibrium. Another tendency is to reduce the person to moral performance: “I am what I do.” Holiness is measured by visible compliance, and salvation is functionally framed as behavior management. A third reduction leans toward materialism: “I am my body and brain.” Human beings are treated as complex biological systems, and spiritual language becomes either metaphorical or marginal. Each of these impulses contains a partial truth: feelings matter; actions matter; embodiment matters. Yet taken as governing frames, they cannot sustain a properly Christian account of salvation. If the self is exhausted by feeling or performance, then salvation will be imagined merely as emotional relief or moral improvement. If the human being is only a biological machine, then talk of communion with God, deification, or participation in Christ becomes unintelligible. In each case, ecclesial life shrinks: worship is reduced to inspiration, ethics to technique, and pastoral care to adjustment. These prior answers also neglect the ecclesial, sacramental, and eschatological dimensions of the gospel. The Church becomes a support group or an ethical society, rather than the body that participates in Christ’s healed humanity and lives toward the resurrection. The sacraments are treated as symbols of our inner states rather than as means by which the Spirit unites us to Christ. The eschatological horizon of likeness to God is obscured behind immediate needs and projects. Section Summary: Psychological, moralistic, and materialist reductions each grasp something real but finally prove inadequate: they cannot sustain Scripture’s portrayal of humanity as image-bearing, sin-wounded, and ordered to participation in God through Christ and the Spirit. These frames truncate both the scope of salvation and the depth of ecclesial life. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: “salvation” is emotional relief, moral performance, or successful coping within the limits of the present age. After: salvation is participation in Christ’s healed humanity, within the Church, ordered toward deification and resurrection.
docs.title: II. Prior Answers and Their Inadequacy

docs.text: Genesis 1:26–27 announces the human as created in the image and likeness of God. From the beginning, humanity is constituted by divine address, entrusted with dominion, and oriented toward a destiny of likeness. This is not a static possession but a vocation: to grow into the likeness of the God whose image we bear. Even after the fall, Scripture never says that the image is lost; rather, the image is wounded and obscured. Human life now unfolds under conditions of misdirected desire, distorted perception, and disordered rule. The gospel does not begin with human striving but with God’s decisive act: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). In Jesus Christ, the eternal Son assumes our nature without ceasing to be who he is. His life, death, and resurrection manifest human nature as it is meant to be—filial, eucharistic, and oriented wholly to the Father. In him we see not an escape from created finitude, but a redeemed and glorified humanity that is the template and source of our renewal. Scripture ties this renewal to a transformation of perception and understanding. The risen Christ “opened their minds ( nous ) to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45), and Paul exhorts believers: “Be transformed by the renewal of your mind ( nous )” (Rom 12:2). Here the nous is not bare intellect but the deep “eye of the heart” by which the whole person attends to reality. As we behold “the glory of the Lord” we are “being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Cor 3:18); we “have stripped off the old self with its practices and have clothed [ourselves] with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator” (Col 3:9–10). Section Summary: Scripture presents humanity as created in God’s image and called to likeness, wounded but not erased by sin, and renewed through the incarnate Son who assumes and perfects our nature and opens the nous to God’s reality. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: the human problem is primarily behavioral or emotional, requiring better rules or better feelings. After: the human problem is a wounded image and darkened nous ; the solution is God’s assumption and renewal of our nature in Christ, and the Spirit’s transformation of perception and desire.
docs.title: III. The Scriptural Event or Claim

docs.text: The patristic tradition reads Genesis and the gospel narratives not as isolated texts but as parts of a single economy of salvation. A widespread interpretation distinguishes between “image” and “likeness”: the image is a structural gift given in creation, while likeness is an eschatological telos —the journey into mature communion with God. Gregory of Nyssa , in On the Making of Man , portrays human life as an infinite progression into divine likeness, grounded in the unlosable image. Within this broad consensus, one influential strand—especially in Maximus the Confessor —discerns within the image a triadic pattern corresponding to a kind of Trinitarian anthropology: nous , logos , and pneuma . The nous is the spiritual perception or “eye of the heart”; the logos is rational articulation and meaning-making; and the pneuma is the vital dynamism of the person in love and movement. Sin is thus more than rule-breaking: it is the misorientation of the whole human life—clouded nous , distorted logos , dissipated pneuma . Athanasius famously summarizes the incarnational horizon: “God became man that man might become god” ( On the Incarnation 54). Deification ( theosis ) does not mean absorption into the divine essence, but participation in God’s life through the Son’s restored humanity. Augustine , Cyril of Alexandria , and John of Damascus each, in distinctive ways, emphasize that the image’s healing and elevation occur in and through Christ, within the Church, by the Spirit. Taken together, the Fathers read Scripture as revealing an anthropology ordered to deification, grounded in Christ’s person and work. Section Summary: The Fathers discern in Scripture an anthropology in which the image is retained but wounded, ordered to likeness, and structured by nous–logos–pneuma ; they interpret Christ’s incarnate and deifying work as the healing and elevation of this image within the Church. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: modern habits read Scripture as a set of religious ideas about an isolated individual self. After: the Church’s patristic reading unveils a coherent economy in which human nous–logos–pneuma are healed and deified through union with the incarnate Son.
docs.title: IV. Patristic Reading and Insight

docs.text: The Council of Chalcedon (451) confesses Christ as one divine person ( hypostasis ) in two natures ( physeis ), “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.” This distinction clarifies that nature answers the question what something is, while person answers who . Applied to anthropology, it yields two guardrails: we must neither reduce persons to functions (psychology, biology, or sheer will) nor treat “person” as a disembodied ghost. A human person is an irreducible “who” who subsists as embodied, ensouled human nature. Christ is the key. In him, the eternal “who” of the Son truly assumes the human “what” of our nature without diminishing either. The gospel, then, is not the rescue of souls from bodies, nor the enhancement of a generic spirituality, but the healing and glorification of humanity in the incarnate Son. Here we can distinguish an objective and a personal dimension: objectively, human nature is healed, clarified, and perfected in the economy of the incarnate Word; personally, each human hypostasis is united to Christ and transformed by the Spirit. Deification thus has both a Christological center and a pneumatological extension. This doctrinal synthesis allows a non-reductionist anthropology. The person is more than psyche, body, or will, yet never exists apart from them. Human nature, assumed and renewed in Christ, is the site where salvation is enacted; persons participate in this renewed nature through union with Christ by the Spirit, especially in the Church’s sacramental and liturgical life. Chalcedonian Christology thus becomes a key for understanding both who the human person is and how salvation truly heals and elevates our being. Section Summary: By reading Scripture with the Church, we arrive at a Chalcedonian anthropology: persons are irreducible “who’s” who subsist in human nature; this nature is assumed, healed, and glorified in Christ; and each person is called to participate personally in this renewed humanity through the Spirit. Frame Shift (Before → After): Before: we could not speak coherently about salvation without either collapsing the person into nature (biology, psychology, will) or dissolving nature into a vague “self.” After: we can confess and live an anthropology in which human nature is objectively renewed in Christ and each person is personally united to him by the Spirit.

docs.text: Chapter 4 — Telos: Covenantal Love Thesis (≤2 sentences): The telos of covenantal‑liturgical participation is love—embodied, enacted, sacrificial, communal, and eschatological: love of God that becomes obedience, and love of neighbor that becomes mercy and reconciliation (Deut 6:4–9; Mark 12:29–34; John 14:15–21; Heb 13:1–16). Because the Church is a Covenant–Temple people formed by Christ the living Mercy Seat and the Spirit’s God‑active presence, love is not a sentiment but the mature fruit of communion, the “true sacrifice” that endures into the age to come (1 Cor 13:8–13; Gal 5:22–25; Rom 12:1–2). Biblical Ground (passages): Deut 6:4–9; Lev 19:9–18; Ps 51:16–17; Mic 6:6–8; Hos 6:6; Matt 5:21–24, 43–48; Matt 7:16–20, 24–27; Matt 22:34–40; Mark 12:29–34; Luke 10:25–37; John 13:34–35; John 14:15–24; John 15:9–17; Rom 5:5; Rom 12:1–21; 1 Cor 13:1–13; 2 Cor 5:14–21; Gal 5:6, 13–25; Eph 4:1–6; Eph 5:1–2; Heb 10:19–25; Heb 13:1–16; 1 John 3:16–18; 1 John 4:7–21; Rev 21:1–5; Rev 22:1–5. Argument Map (Wilken‑calibrated): [Setup/Context → Question‑at‑Issue → Prior Answers (insufficient) → Scripture/Event Anchor → Patristic Turn → Doctrinal Resolution (Synthesis) → Payoff/Implications] One‑liners for each move (keep it tight) Setup/Context: Covenant and Temple exist to form a priestly people who dwell with God; therefore the goal cannot be mere correctness but communion expressed as love (Exod 19:5–6; Deut 6:4–9; 1 Pet 2:5, 9). Question‑at‑Issue: If Christ fulfills the Mercy Seat and the Spirit forms participation, what is the end toward which this participation trains the renewed nous and orders the Church’s life? (Rom 12:1–2; John 15:9–10). Prior Answers: (1) legalism (telos as rule‑keeping); (2) moralism (telos as human achievement); (3) sentimentalism (telos as feeling)—each fails to account for love as covenantal, sacrificial, and eschatological (Hos 6:6; 1 Cor 13:1–3, 8). Scripture/Event Anchor: Jesus unites love of God and love of neighbor as the covenant’s summary; love is defined as obedience and self‑gift, anchored in His own cross (Mark 12:29–31; John 14:15; 15:13; 1 John 3:16). Patristic Turn: Augustine orders love; Irenaeus frames love as maturation toward likeness; Gregory of Nyssa and Maximus show love as participation’s end; Chrysostom insists Eucharistic love must become almsgiving; Basil locates mercy as the liturgy beyond the liturgy (Rom 5:5; Heb 13:16). Doctrinal Resolution: The Church confesses that love is the telos because God is love and because covenantal‑liturgical participation is communion with the Triune God; the Spirit pours love into our hearts, and the ordo trains that love into embodied mercy and reconciliation (1 John 4:7–12; Rom 5:5; Gal 5:6). Rom 3:25–26). If the Covenant–Temple pattern has a purpose, it cannot terminate in external conformity. It must terminate in communion—and communion, in Scripture, is named as love. The Shema names Israel’s telos with liturgical clarity: “Hear… You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deut 6:4–5). Hearing is not preliminary; it is the first act of love, because covenant begins with divine speech and human Amen (Exod 24:3–8; Deut 6:6–9). Likewise the prophets insist that worship detached from mercy becomes contradiction: God desires steadfast love and not sacrifice, mercy and not empty offering (Hos 6:6; Mic 6:6–8). The temple’s purpose is not to protect religious performance but to produce a people whose life mirrors God’s own character. In the prologue’s first lenses we have already been told why this can occur. Christ is the living Mercy Seat, the place where justice and mercy meet (Rom 3:25–26), and the Spirit is God‑active, forming participation through the ordo (Acts 2:42; 1 Cor 10:16–17). The third lens named the human organ that can receive this training: the renewed nous (Rom 12:2; 1 Cor 2:16). Now the fourth lens names the end: the telos is covenantal love—sacrificial, enacted, and enduring. Question‑at‑Issue: What is the end of participation—what is it for? The Church confesses much that is true: Christ fulfills the Temple, the Spirit constitutes the Church, and the ordo mediates communion. Yet the doctrinal question is incomplete until we ask: for what end? What is participation aimed at? Scripture answers by making an audacious claim: the goal of divine presence is not merely that we may be spared judgment but that we may be made capable of love—love that images God and becomes the Church’s “true sacrifice” (Rom 12:1; Heb 13:15–16). Therefore we ask: What is the telos toward which covenantal‑liturgical participation trains the renewed nous and orders the Church’s corporate life? (John 15:9–10; 1 Cor 13:8–13). If the telos is misunderstood, everything else becomes distorted. The ordo becomes technique; doctrine becomes identity‑badge; ethics becomes either anxious striving or permissive drift. But if the telos is named rightly, the lenses cohere: Christ opens the way, the Spirit forms participation, the nous is trained to perceive, and love becomes the mature fruit. Prior Answers (why insufficient): Three rival teloi that hollow the covenant Three distortions compete for the position of “end.” Legalism: telos as rule‑keeping. Here the covenant is reduced to external compliance. Yet Jesus locates the covenant’s core not in mere prohibition but in love of God and neighbor (Mark 12:29–31). The prophets’ critique exposes the defect: sacrifice without mercy is void (Hos 6:6). Legalism can produce control, but it cannot produce covenantal love. Moralism: telos as human achievement. Here love becomes a heroic virtue we manufacture, and liturgy becomes motivational fuel. Paul’s grammar contradicts this: love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom 5:5), and fruit grows from walking by the Spirit (Gal 5:22–25). Moralism treats love as wage rather than gift‑made‑habit. Sentimentalism: telos as feeling. Here love is equated with warmth or affirmation. But Scripture defines love as fidelity, obedience, and self‑gift: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15), and “greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life” (John 15:13). Love is cruciform, covenantal, and costly. Each distortion fails because it severs love from participation in God’s own life. The Church must therefore retrieve the biblical claim: love is not merely commanded; it is enacted by Christ, poured by the Spirit, trained by the ordo, and oriented toward the eschatological consummation where God dwells with His people (Rev 21:3–4). Scripture/Event Anchor: Jesus sums the covenant; the cross defines love; the Spirit supplies it Jesus does not invent a new telos; He reveals the covenant’s inner meaning. When asked about the greatest commandment, He answers by joining the Shema with Leviticus: love of God and love of neighbor are one fabric (Mark 12:29–31; Lev 19:18). This is not a summary that replaces the law; it is the law’s heart. The covenant is ordered toward a people who love God wholly and therefore love neighbor concretely. Jesus then defines love’s form by His own self‑gift. The new commandment—“love one another as I have loved you”—is given in the shadow of the Passion (John 13:34–35). Love is not merely “be nice”; it is “as I have loved,” and the measure of that love is the cross (John 15:13; 1 John 3:16). Therefore covenantal love is sacrificial by definition: it is the willingness to give oneself for the other. The New Testament also defines love’s power. Paul says love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom 5:5). This locates love within the prologue’s second lens: the Spirit is God‑active. Love is not an autonomous human resource; it is participation in divine life communicated by the Spirit (Gal 5:22). Thus even when love appears as command—“walk in love” (Eph 5:2)—it is simultaneously gift: the Spirit forms what He commands. Finally, Hebrews ties love to worship’s logic. The Church draws near through Christ and is exhorted to consider how to “stir up one another to love and good works,” refusing isolation (Heb 10:19–25). Worship is therefore not an escape from ethics; it is the furnace where love is kindled and trained. Hebrews 13 makes the consequence explicit: “Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God” (Heb 13:16). The altar of the New Covenant issues in the sacrifice of mercy. Patristic Turn: Love as the Church’s interpretive rule, sacrificial offering, and eschatological end The Fathers do not sentimentalize love; they thicken it. Augustine insists that caritas is the rule of reading and the ordering principle of life. In On Christian Doctrine , he famously argues that all interpretation aims at love of God and neighbor; if an interpretation does not build love, it has missed the point. This aligns with Jesus’ own summary (Mark 12:29–31). Augustine’s “ordered love” protects against both legalism and sentimentalism: love has an object (God first), a shape (obedience), and a direction (neighbor). Irenaeus frames love within divine pedagogy. Humanity is formed over time toward likeness, and that likeness is not bare rationality but filial communion—life in which love becomes possible because God first loved and healed (cf. 1 John 4:10–11). Irenaeus thereby anchors telos in participation: God’s purpose is not to produce moral performers but mature sons and daughters who share His life. Gregory of Nyssa shows love’s eschatological depth. If the human being is made for the vision of God (Matt 5:8), then love is the movement of the whole person toward God—ever‑deepening desire, purified and enlarged. Love is not exhausted by achievement; it expands into glory, which is why Paul can say love never ends (1 Cor 13:8). Maximus makes the connection between liturgy and love explicit. For him, the end of ascetic struggle and ecclesial participation is the unification of the person and the Church in self‑giving love. Love is the sign that the faculties have been healed and that the Church is living from communion rather than rivalry (Phil 2:1–5). This makes love not optional ethics but the proof of true participation. Chrysostom adds pastoral severity: the Table demands mercy. His preaching refuses the division between Eucharistic realism and social indifference. If we receive Christ’s Body, we must recognize His Body in the poor; otherwise the liturgy becomes condemnation rather than communion (cf. 1 Cor 11:27–29). Chrysostom thereby enforces altar‑logic: reconciliation and almsgiving are liturgical consequences (Matt 5:23–24). Basil likewise frames mercy as sacrifice. In his social homilies, he treats hoarding as theft from the poor, precisely because possessions are entrusted for love. Basil’s vision is not political slogan but covenantal logic: God’s people are a priesthood, and priesthood entails offering—now expressed as sharing, hospitality, and justice (Heb 13:16; Mic 6:8). The Fathers therefore read Scripture in harmony: love is the interpretive rule, the sacrificial consequence, and the eschatological end of participation. Doctrinal Resolution (Synthesis): Love as telos because covenant is communion with the God who is love The synthesis can now be stated in seven linked claims. God is love; therefore communion with God is communion with love. John’s claim is not mere attribute language: “God is love” (1 John 4:8). To participate in God’s life is to be drawn into love as reality. Covenant is ordered toward communion; communion is expressed as obedient love. The Shema binds hearing to love (Deut 6:4–9), and Jesus binds love to obedience (John 14:15). Love is therefore covenantal allegiance made visible. Christ defines love’s form as sacrificial self‑gift. Love is “as I have loved you” (John 13:34), and His love culminates in laying down His life (John 15:13). Therefore love’s shape is cruciform. The Spirit supplies love’s power and makes it habitual. Love is poured into our hearts (Rom 5:5) and appears as fruit (Gal 5:22). The Spirit does not merely demand love; He forms it as participation. The ordo trains love by retraining the nous and desire. Worship is pedagogy: we are transformed by renewing the mind (Rom 12:1–2), and we are exhorted within assembly to stir one another to love (Heb 10:24–25). Word, Table, Prayer are not religious tasks but the Church’s training ground for love. Love becomes the Church’s “true sacrifice.” Hebrews names praise and sharing as sacrifices pleasing to God (Heb 13:15–16), and Paul frames the whole life as living sacrifice (Rom 12:1). The Covenant–Temple pattern is fulfilled: the offering is now the people offered in Christ through love. Love is eschatological: it alone endures. Paul’s hymn is decisive: prophecies cease, tongues pass away, knowledge fades—“but love never ends” (1 Cor 13:8). Revelation depicts the consummation as God dwelling with His people, wiping tears away (Rev 21:3–4). The telos is not an abstract afterlife but perfected communion—unbroken love. Thus the fourth lens is not an ethical appendix. It is the end that gathers the other lenses: Christ’s Mercy Seat makes love possible by reconciling; the Spirit makes love actual by forming participation; the renewed nous perceives and discerns love’s demands; and the Church becomes the visible sign of the kingdom through embodied mercy. Payoff/Implications (worship/ethics/formation): Love as the liturgy after the liturgy Worship: love as the criterion of true participation. Jesus ties altar and reconciliation: if we bring a gift to the altar and remember a brother has something against us, we must go first and be reconciled (Matt 5:23–24). The Church cannot treat this as mere moral counsel; it is liturgical instruction. The ordo, properly received, forms the Church into a reconciled body that practices peace (Eph 4:1–3). Worship that does not train love is not merely incomplete; it contradicts itself (1 John 4:20–21). Ethics: mercy as sacrificial consequence. Hebrews’ command—do not neglect to share—names the concrete shape of love (Heb 13:16). The Good Samaritan parable embodies the same logic: neighbor‑love is not abstract sentiment but costly action across boundaries (Luke 10:33–35). Such mercy is not optional activism; it is the outward form of inward communion. Formation: a stable habitus ordered to the telos. Paul names love as the one thing that gives value to all gifts (1 Cor 13:1–3) and as the bond of perfection (Col 3:14). Formation therefore aims at a stable person—patient, kind, not envious—because these are the features of a life participating in God’s own love (Gal 5:22–23). In this way, the Covenant–Temple pattern becomes daily existence: the Church’s liturgy trains a people whose lives become offerings, and whose offerings are love. This completes the prologue’s four lenses as a single rule of reading: Christ is the key; the Spirit is formative power; the nous is the organ of perception; and the telos is covenantal love. Everything that follows in Parts I–IX will unfold what this love looks like in sacred time, in the ordo, in households, in economy, and in suffering—until the final city where love is the air we breathe (Rev 22:1–5). Objections & Replies: [3–5 strongest] Objection: “If love is the telos, does doctrine become secondary?” Reply: Scripture binds truth and love rather than separating them. Jesus joins the greatest commandments to right confession (“The Lord is one,” Mark 12:29) and Paul insists that love rejoices with the truth (1 Cor 13:6). Doctrine is ordered toward communion; love is the mature form of that communion. To detach doctrine from love is to misunderstand doctrine’s purpose (1 Tim 1:5). Objection: “Isn’t ‘love’ too vague to function as a theological end?” Reply: Biblical love is concrete and covenantal: love of God is expressed in obedience (John 14:15), love of neighbor is expressed in mercy and action (1 John 3:16–18), and love’s form is defined by the cross (John 15:13). Paul further specifies love’s features (1 Cor 13:4–7). The telos is not vague; it is cruciform and practical. Objection: “If love is poured by the Spirit (Rom 5:5), why command it at all?” Reply: Scripture’s commands are not mere demands but invitations into participation. The Spirit forms what is commanded, and the Church learns to “walk by the Spirit” so that love becomes fruit (Gal 5:16, 22). Command without gift would be despair; gift without command would be aimless. The covenant holds both: God acts, and the people respond (Phil 2:12–13). Objection: “Does focusing on mercy risk turning the Church into a social‑service agency?” Reply: Hebrews frames mercy as sacrifice flowing from worship (Heb 13:15–16), and Jesus frames reconciliation as altar‑logic (Matt 5:23–24). Mercy is therefore not a substitute for worship but its consequence. Chrysostom’s insistence guards the priority: the Church gives because she communes; she does not commune because she gives. Objection: “Love as telos sounds like ‘be nice’—how does it address justice and holiness?” Reply: Biblical love includes holiness and truth: it refuses evil and rejoices in truth (1 Cor 13:6), it seeks reconciliation and justice (Matt 5:23–24; Mic 6:8), and it even loves enemies without denying wrongdoing (Matt 5:44–48). Covenantal love is not permissiveness; it is sacrificial fidelity to God that becomes mercy toward neighbor. Annotated Bibliography (SBL): - Hays, Richard B. The Moral Vision of the New Testament: Community, Cross, New Creation . San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 1996. (Connects ethics to ecclesial participation and cross‑shaped love; strong on communal formation.) - de Lubac, Henri. Catholicism: Christ and the Common Destiny of Man . Trans. Lancelot C. Sheppard and Elizabeth Englund. San Francisco: Ignatius Press, 1988. (Classic ressourcement on ecclesial communion and love as the Church’s social ontology.) - Nygren, Anders. Agape and Eros . Trans. Philip S. Watson. London: SPCK, 1953. (Historically influential; helpful as a conversation partner for clarifying love’s biblical shape, though requires critical reading.) - O’Donovan, Oliver. Resurrection and Moral Order: An Outline for Evangelical Ethics . 2nd ed. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1994. (Ethics grounded in Christ’s resurrection; clarifies how obedience and love relate.) - Ratzinger, Joseph (Benedict XVI). Deus Caritas Est . San Francisco: Ignatius Press, 2006. (Concise theological synthesis of love’s divine source and ecclesial expression; bridges patristic and modern retrieval.) - Wright, N. T. After You Believe: Why Christian Character Matters . New York: HarperOne, 2010. (Virtue/formation account that aligns with “fruit” logic—habitus shaped by worship and communal practice.)
